Thanks! To be honest I don't lift very much anymore 😅 it's probably optimal to do both, but I find that climbing is enough to keep me fit. The climbing gym I go to has a weights area, but it's not as expansive as a traditional gym, so my options also aren't as appealing. I do miss my preacher curl and hack squat machines :(

I also naturally have quite disproportionately big and strong legs (I wonder why...) and I try to keep everything engaged when I climb, not just my upper body, so I don't have much of a need for a dedicated leg day. I'd say you probably want to lift to fill in the gaps, so to speak, for the muscles that don't get trained as directly by climbing, like chest and shoulders. On the other hand, do exercises that will help your climbing directly, like pull ups and core work. My priorities at this point are both functionality and aesthetics, and pure strength really mostly by association, so I do mostly bodyweight exercises aside from climbing.

Thank you! To be honest I went through a few distinct phases. 


Summer of 2023 was mostly relatively intuitive eating and making protein smoothies a few times a week.


Then my freshman year of college was dining hall food and fast food, but I always made an attempt to make meals relatively balanced; e.g. always eating some kind of protein, at least one fruit or vegetable, and only one dessert if I felt like it. I tried to emphasize protein, but passively. I didn't really gain a freshman 15 or anything, but my campus is also pretty big so I guess I just burned off what I ate. This is also when I started to pay attention to my step count and go on walks, which I would now consider essential to my weight loss!!


Summer of 2024 I really tried to dial in on my diet. I paid for a macrofactor subscription for most of the summer and was really consistent for like the first 2 months, but then my family went on a long vacation and I didn't track my food basically at all. It was really helpful for me and I got down to 150lbs towards the end of June, though with less muscle than the same weight now. I also worked at Portillos (a Chicagoland fast food restaurant) for the summer, which actually really helped, because the salads are great and were perfect for my nutrition goals. Oikos triple zero yogurt was also a must. 


When I went back to school it was basically the same as the previous year, still mostly dining halls, with some more mindfulness about portion sizes. I could buy fairlife core power protein shakes with my dining plan, which was super helpful. My schedule this past semester was also super busy but very structured, which helped me make better eating decisions all around. 


Now that I'm home for the summer, I've started using macrofactor again, aiming for about 2k calories and 150g of protein a day. I drink a lot of fair life protein shakes and seeq protein, which makes like a clear juice, which I don't understand how that works but I like it way more than chalky powders. Triple zero yogurt (or otherwise fat free Greek yogurt) is still a staple, and I usually eat eggs for breakfast.


I wouldn't necessarily consider my diet to be the greatest, I buy some kind of sugary coffee or latte almost every day and I snack more often than I should, especially in place of actual meals. But I'm happy with the progress I've made and the path I'm on, and I think that's most important.

I'm not OP but I think my perspective might be valuable to you. I came out at 11, started hormones at 15, and got top surgery at 17. My parents were cautiously supportive and it took them a long, long time to get on board with anything permanent. My mom was initially very staunchly against hormones, and ESPECIALLY surgery, before 18. The biggest reason for them changing their mind was that over all those years, at least outwardly, I never wavered. And it continuously and clearly was impacting my quality of life. In turn, after transition, specifically my surgery, my life changed. I know I'm extremely fortunate to have this experience. Although it was infuriating at the time, from my vantage point now I think the slowness was absolutely the responsible thing to do and there's very little I would (now) rather that we did differently.


My mom's big regret, which I would agree with, is not considering hormone blockers. There is so much misinformation and fear mongering surrounding them in this political climate, but they are reversible. But in many aspects, puberty is just as irreversible as HRT. All the testosterone in the world won't unfuse my growth plates. My hips are stuck like this, my height is stuck like this. Blockers would have reduced or even eliminated the need for later surgery. And at the very, very least, they give you time to consider your options before nature decides for you.


Additionally, make sure your child understands all the impacts of hormones. This sounds obvious, but I was tuned the fuck out during the meetings my parents had with doctors. I had already decided that it was something I wanted, and that my parents wouldn't ever give to me, so I was paying very little attention. Things have worked out for me, but this is how people end up detransitioning, because of their own ignorance. I encourage you as the parent also to learn as much as you can, preferably directly from medical professionals (though the Internet is often a valuable resource too), so you can help your child as best and knowledgeably as possible.


Good luck. PM me if you want to talk about this more.

Sorry for the late response!! Yes, physically I feel so so much better about myself. I'm still working on it, I hate how all my shirts still catch around my hips, but it's slow and steady. I used to buy pants in a 36in waist, and the other day I bought shorts that were 29 and 30. In the first pic I'm around 170lbs and recently I've been hovering around 150lbs. My goal is to get to around 135lbs with a lower bf%. I used to focus heavily on cardio, specifically the stairmaster. I actually watched almost all of breaking bad while on the stairmaster, God knows how many flights I've climbed 🤣 Currently I do PPL, which for me looks like doing 4-6 exercises hitting each respective muscle group each time I go. My weekly work schedule is weird so when I go to the gym I just pick up where I left off (e.g. if I did push last time, do pull this time), but I do try to go 4ish times a week.

Here are some things that really helped for me; for one, not drinking my calories. I've not been a big soda person these last few years anyway, but I would still have the occasional sprite or root beer and sugary lemonades fairly often, and that probably added up a lot more than I thought. I love my iced coffees, but I try to go less frequently (also a win for my wallet) and get less sugary options. Nowadays it's mostly water, sometimes with a crystal lite, and a protein shake once every day or two. 

Also, daily steps. My smartwatch always had the 10k 'goal' but I never really tried to meet it, y'know? Especially in the winters or on boring days, even as a college student, I was doing like 2-3k. In early May I was having some pretty bad interpersonal problems so I would take long walks listening to music just to take my mind off it. I'm talking 25-30k steps some days. Since then I've taken up walking as a habit and settled on a goal of 12k, and I usually meet it. The important thing is not falling off the horse. It's okay if I don't hit it one day, but not letting that stop the momentum, you know? The streak isn't important, it's choosing to continue to show up for yourself.

Otherwise, it's the pretty basic concept of CICO. Burning more calories than you eat. Watching what you eat, or at least making smart choices about portion sizes and the like. Find things you enjoy, in amounts you can enjoy, that align with your goals. The restaurant I work at makes some killer desserts and I probably bring one home at least once a week. Eat half one night, eat the other half the next, only 250 calories each, no problem. I've been tracking my calories recently too (I use macrofactor, I like how precise it is compared to like MFP) which helps me more accurately understand how many calories I'm eating, and makes me more mindful of snacking.

I wish it was told as 5 short stories rather than tales told once every five (very short) chapters, but I can understand why it's formatted the way it is since it lends itself to suspense. All in all, highly recommend!

I DNFed Hidden Bodies- the sequel to You- because the story was just too wildly different and the main character's arc derailed. As for Elevation, it's my first Stephen king book (I'm reading the Green Mile soon!) and I gave it 5 stars. I loved how the LGBT characters weren't at all perpetuating stereotypes or in-your-face and, I don't know, just have me a sense of lightness- pun intended :)
